points: Open-source software maintained by the WordPress community. Many hosting companies offer managed installations.
PHP runs on the server. MySQL or MariaDB stores posts, settings, and user accounts.
Editors use a browser-based block editor. Visitors receive HTML, CSS, and JavaScript from the active theme.
Editors can build pages from reusable blocks.
Themes control the layout. Plugins add features such as forms or online stores. A REST API lets other applications read or update content.
A self-hosted site needs ongoing updates for the core software, themes, and plugins.
An abandoned plugin can leave a site dependent on code that no longer receives security fixes.
Open-source project maintained by the Drupal community. The Drupal Association supports the project, and service providers offer commercial support.
PHP runs on the server. Supported databases include MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, and SQLite.
Editors manage content in a browser. Twig templates generate the HTML visitors see.
Administrators can define content types with different fields, such as a school event with a date, location, and organizer.
Roles, editorial workflows, and translations let departments manage and approve their own content.
Someone must design the content types, permissions, and workflows before editors can use them.
Major upgrades require checking whether contributed modules and custom themes work with the new release.
Open-source software developed by the nonprofit Ghost Foundation. Ghost(Pro) is its managed hosting service.
Node.js runs the application. MySQL 8 is the supported production database.
Writers use the browser editor. Handlebars themes render the publication for readers.
Publish an article to the website, send it as an email newsletter, or do both.
Offer free and paid memberships and restrict individual posts to specific membership tiers.
Built-in paid subscriptions depend on Stripe. A publisher that needs another payment processor must arrange a separate integration.
Self-hosting requires maintaining the Node.js application and its database.
Open-source CMS created by Torchbox and maintained with community contributors. Commercial development and support are available.
Built on Python and Django. PostgreSQL is a supported production database.
Editors work in a browser admin interface. Django templates can render pages for visitors.
Developers define page types and the blocks editors can combine, such as text, images, and quotations.
Editors can preview changes and submit pages for approval before publishing.
Setting up a site requires coding skills. A new page type generally requires a developer to define its fields and template.
Open-source CMS maintained by the Grav team and community. The team also offers paid products and support.
PHP runs on the server. Markdown and YAML files store page content and settings without a database server.
Twig templates render HTML. A browser-based admin interface is available for editors.
Themes and plugins extend the site. Editors can publish multilingual pages.
Because content is stored in files, a team can track page changes in Git alongside its templates.
Grav does not provide relational tables for page content. A project that needs SQL joins across records would need a separate data layer.
A static-only host cannot run Grav's PHP application directly.
